posts.title: Jab We Met
posts.excerpt: I have watched this movie more than 30 times, and somehow I still find something in Aditya and Geet that stays with me.
posts.review:
Geet gives Aditya the open space he needed. She opens up about herself, and somehow that makes him feel comfortable enough to talk about what he is going through when they meet. Later, they bond because both of them reciprocate so naturally.

He was broken, cheated on and at one of the lowest points of his life, yet he still chose his morals. He was with her in fucking Ratlam, in his darkest phase, with so many setbacks, and he still decided to go all in and get her home. Somewhere along the way, he realised the beauty, aura, innocence, sweetness and purity that Geet carries.

I feel like he might have fallen in love with her even before she told him about Anshuman. I know this because at one point in my life, I used to think that people who came into my life during my lowest phases were some kind of sign from the universe that they were meant to love me. I know now that it was completely wrong. They were probably just sent to teach me some lessons. It's crazy how God knows everything.

And I do believe Aditya fell in love with her, but because he knew she loved someone else, he stopped himself. Instead, he worked on himself. It wasn't Geet who gave him the power to rebuild himself. She just listened to him and 'pakkaaved' him with her talks. She gave him the space to open up and find himself again.

And he trusted, loved and believed in her so much that he left her, hoping she would be fine with the guy she was in love with. Then, when he gets her back, he could have easily proclaimed his love and said, "I have grown, be mine." But even then, he chose to hear what she felt before entering her territory.

He chose to be humane instead of overpowering her.

He helped her recover and get back to her family yet again. And finally, she wisely chose Aditya over the guy who thought she was crazy and didn't even care enough to check whether the girl who had left everything for him was okay or not.

I have watched this movie more than 30 times, and honestly, I think I was searching for Aditya for a very long time.

It was only after watching 'BKU' that I realised that.

posts.title: Obsession
posts.excerpt: The first time I watched it, I saw it one way. The second time, it almost felt like a completely different movie.
posts.review:
It shows how anything in excess isn't good. The guy has feelings for her, and she gets to know it. That's how girls are, we just somehow know these things. She even asks him directly if he has feelings for her, but he gets flustered and says no. Then he wishes for her to become obsessed with him and fall deeply in love with him.

And that's where he gets the karma for asking for too much.

I could see all those little things girls do when they are in love, but because he wished for obsession instead of just normal love, she starts doing everything to an extreme.

I actually liked the ending. I feel like the guy could have gotten a second chance for the mistake he made, but then again, life isn't always fair. He dies in the end, and the girl, completely consumed by her obsession and rage, ends up killing her two friends. In all that trauma, the guy kills himself, and the wish that had turned into wrath and ruined the lives of four people is finally released. The girl who was possessed by that wish comes back to normal.

That was my insight when I watched the movie for the first time. But when I watched it again, I had a completely different perspective. It almost felt like I was watching a different movie altogether.

I do feel, though, that the way the storyline is presented makes it feel more like watching a vlog than an actual movie.

posts.title: Sexing the Cherry
posts.excerpt: I really liked this book, especially because the female lead stayed in my mind much more than anything else in it.
posts.review:
I really liked Sexing the Cherry. What stood out to me first was the time in which the story is set, seventeenth-century London. I wasn't really aware of how things were back then. I used to feel that because London is such a hyped city, things must always have been perfect there, but that was clearly not the case.

What stayed with me the most was the female lead. She is fierce, bold and very open. She knows herself well and always takes a stand for herself. She is honest and bold, especially for a time when women were so suppressed.

The book has disturbing and harsh realities, but she is bold enough to voice herself every time. Even though she didn't really have financial freedom, she still felt independent, and I think that is what made me admire her so much.

Later, the story moves to Jordan's point of view, and he too seems to understand his mother more with time. He also falls in love with a girl, though I honestly don't remember that part very clearly. Maybe that is because I was so amazed by the female lead that she remained the strongest part of the book for me.

posts.title: The Liberation of Sita
posts.excerpt: I had never really come across our mythological stories from the female point of view before this, and that is what made this book stay with me.
posts.review:
I was amazed while reading this book. I had never really come across our mythological stories from the female point of view, and I was genuinely happy with how this was brought about.

This is a very individualistic topic, but I really loved how Sita Mata interacted with these women and how their point of view was narrated.

Starting with Surpanakha, I myself had always assumed that she was the villain. But while reading her story, she seemed so naive to me. Yes, it was her mistake to approach a man who was already married, but I don't think that should have led to her losing her beauty. I don't believe external beauty is everything, but women carry immense beauty in their physical appearance. People have often considered it a weakness or a form of allurement, but that is also simply a part of who she is. Women carry beauty along with great strength, emotional intelligence and empathy.

Then comes Ahalya, whose mistake seemed to be her beauty. Her husband was a sage, yet he didn't trust her enough before cursing her.

Next was Renuka, Parashurama's mother. I had never heard much about her before reading this book. I felt it was unfair of her son to follow his father blindly. Until then, I had respect for Parashurama. I agree that we are all human and learn things with time, but that act was something I really did not expect from such an educated and skilled man.

Then there was Urmila. Before this book, I only knew that she gave her sleep for her husband, but the things she went through were way beyond what I had imagined.

The author brought each of these women's perspectives out very well. Through them, Sita slowly understands that she does not have to be the ideal woman when things are really not favouring her. She does not have to keep proving herself or survive in this world by sacrificing everything, including herself.

The journey of learning about oneself, taking a stand for oneself and not being dependent on anyone is what I learnt through this book.

mediaEntries.title: On kindness, boundaries & moving on
mediaEntries.text:
I've had this same opinion for a long time. But they got access to our lives because we allowed them to, so I don't think they are completely at fault either.

I've been told several times that I tend to view the world the way I view myself, and I think that is exactly why I've been betrayed on several occasions. I understood what that meant eventually. Being too kind, warm and soft with the wrong people can lead to unnecessary pain and scars that stay with us for a lifetime.

But I also believe we have to forgive them and focus on ourselves. If God, who is superior to all of us, forgives our sins and gives us another day to unlearn, learn and relearn, then who are we to hold on to these trivial matters forever?

And honestly, holding on to feelings from the past can hurt our present more than the people who caused them ever did. To me, that is a bigger blunder than letting these people into our lives in the first place.

I actually appreciate that such people exist in our lives because they teach us that being too kind can also be injurious. There has to be a balance. Sometimes we keep committing to things forever simply because we are constantly thinking about everyone else. But these people teach us that it is okay to take a stand for yourself before anybody else.

There's one catch, though. These ruthless people should have the ability to understand and imbibe the kindness they receive, but most of them never will. And honestly, that's their loss. Because without learning that, they can never really build stable, long-term relationships with people.

We learn, we understand, and we move ahead. That's all.

There's so much more I could add to this. I'll probably add it someday soon.
